soil-water-105.title: Soil loss tolerance, the T value
soil-water-105.text: How much soil can a field lose each year and still be farmed indefinitely? Soil loss tolerance, or the T value, answers in tons per acre per year. It is the maximum average yearly loss that still lets a soil sustain current production economically and indefinitely. T values range from 1 to 5 tons per acre per year. They are calculated with the formula T=υQρC+R(1−C). The agency now called the {{ref:soil-hist-050}} devised it, basing it on the minimum rate of loss that would deplete organic matter and harm crop productivity. In 1961–1962, US soil groups were given T values of 2 to 6 tons per acre per year, later adjusted to 1 to 5. Conservation management adopted it from the mid-1960s. The figures show progress. In 2007, 99 million acres, 28% of US cropland, were eroding faster than T, down from 169 million acres, 40% of cropland, in 1982. Its validity is questioned. Critics note that T values vary across space, may not hold where soluble carbonates abound, as in karst, and should be weighed against actual soil loss.

soil-water-102.title: Riparian buffers, green strips that guard a stream
soil-water-102.text: A nine-year University of Georgia study found that streamside buffers removed at least 60% of the nitrogen and at least 65% of the phosphorus from fertilizer in runoff. A riparian buffer is a vegetated strip beside a stream, usually forested, that shades it and partly shields it from neighboring land use. It intercepts sediment, nutrients, pesticides and other materials in surface runoff, and reduces pollutants in shallow subsurface flow. It also stabilizes the stream bank, so eroding banks take less farmland out of production and less silt reaches lakes and reservoirs downstream. A typical buffer is 15 meters (50 feet) wide on each side, in three zones. Native grasses first slow the runoff, shrubs come next, and fast-growing trees shade the water and hold the bank.

soil-water-095.title: The jet erosion test, scouring soil to measure it
soil-water-095.text: One way to measure a soil's toughness is to aim a jet of water at it and watch the hole grow. The jet erosion test, done in the field or the laboratory, works exactly this way. A turbulent jet strikes the soil at constant hydraulic head. Where its shear stress exceeds the soil's critical value, it scours a hole, whose depth is measured over time. Fitting the erosion rate gives the soil's erodibility and critical shear stress. Engineers use them to design vegetated channels, road embankments, dams, levees and spillways. Its index typically ranges from 0 to 0.03. The method is disputed. Critics question its underlying assumptions, and other erosion tests can give inconsistent erodibility values. As of 2017 no method for soil erodibility was universally accepted. Depending on the fitting method, erodibility for a given critical stress can vary up to 100 times.

soil-water-038.title: Tillage erosion, when the plow moves the hill
soil-water-038.text: The pale, eroded hilltops of many farm fields are often blamed on rain. They are actually caused by the plow. Tillage erosion is soil erosion in cultivated fields caused by the movement of soil during {{ref:soil-agri-095}}. Growing evidence shows that it is a major erosion process on farmland, surpassing water and wind erosion in many fields, especially on sloping and hilly land. It strips organic-rich topsoil from convex spots. Its rate depends on two things. The erosivity of the operation is set by the implement's design, speed and depth. The erodibility of the landscape is set by slope shape and soil properties. The erosion comes from changes, across a field, in translocation, the amount of soil each pass moves. Translocation grows with slope gradient and curvature. Soil is lost from hilltops and from the downslope edges of fields. It piles up in hollows and against field boundaries, building banks of soil. As topsoil thins, plowing mixes poorer subsoil into the plow layer and spreads it across the field, cutting crop productivity for a long time. Soil degraded this way likely becomes more erodible by water and wind. The remedies are lighter cultivation, with fewer, slower and shallower passes and smaller implements, along with contour working, plowing furrows upslope and moving soil back to eroded hilltops.

soil-water-036.title: Dust control, from water trucks to paved lots
soil-water-036.text: Among sites that break dust rules, new urban housing developments are the most frequent violators. Environmental agencies such as the US EPA require facilities that generate fugitive dust to minimize it. Dust control is the suppression of airborne solid particles smaller than 500 micrometers. Construction and demolition sites are sprayed with water, and dust is kept from being tracked onto nearby roads. Unpaved lots and dirt roads are paved or graveled, or stabilized with water, vegetable oil, calcium chloride or other suppressants. The payoff is fewer allergic reactions, cases of pneumonia and asthma attacks, along with better visibility and road safety.

soil-water-110.title: Revegetation, putting plants back on bare ground
soil-water-110.text: Land stripped by wildfire, mining or floods needs plants back before its soil washes away. Revegetation is the replanting and rebuilding of the soil of disturbed land. It may happen naturally, as plants colonize and succession unfolds, or people may carry it out to repair the damage. Preventing erosion is usually the main reason. Plants hold the soil, help it absorb water in heavy rain and sharply reduce turbidity, or cloudiness, in nearby waters. Early practice simply applied seed and fertilizer, usually grasses or clover, whose fibrous roots give short-term erosion control on slopes. Restoring mined land may need soil to be amended, replaced or created. Mycorrhizal fungi are important to success, since most woody plants need them.

soil-water-113.title: Bringing back the tallgrass prairie
soil-water-113.text: By 1849, settlers had plowed up so much tallgrass prairie that most of its grass species had given way to crops. The soil lost the grasses' extensive fibrous roots. Prairie restoration is the work of returning prairie destroyed by industrial, agricultural, commercial or residential development to its earlier state. It helps conserve topsoil, which is exposed to wind and rain erosion once prairie is plowed under. Prairie grasses also take carbon from the air by photosynthesis and store it in the soil, which makes prairie soil useful for locking carbon away. In Europe, former cropland is restored by spontaneous succession, sowing seed mixtures, transferring plant material, and removing and transferring topsoil.

soil-water-109.title: Grassed waterways, green lines down the valley floor
soil-water-109.text: Storm runoff from cropland gathers along the lowest line of a valley. There it can cut rills and gullies that speed the water on and worsen the damage downstream. A grassed waterway guards that line against erosion. It is a strip of native grassland 2 to 48 meters (6.6 to 157.5 feet) wide, laid along the floor of a cultivated dry valley. The grass raises soil cohesion and roughness, prevents rills and gullies, slows runoff and lets it soak back in during long winter rains. It cannot reabsorb runoff from heavy spring and summer storms, so earthen dams across it may be added to hold the flow back for a while. Vegetative filter strips are different. They are narrower, only a few meters wide, and placed along rivers or along or within fields.

soil-water-111.title: WEPP, the physics-based heir to the USLE
soil-water-111.text: An interagency team built WEPP to replace the Universal Soil Loss Equation. Released publicly in 1995, it is now widely used in the United States and elsewhere. WEPP, the Water Erosion Prediction Project model, is a physically based erosion simulation built on hydrology, plant science, hydraulics and erosion mechanics. It takes climate, topography, soil and management inputs. It returns the water balance, soil detachment and deposition along the slope, sediment delivery and vegetation growth. It runs for single storms or continuously, on hillslopes, roads and small parcels, or on whole watersheds of linked hillslopes, channels and impoundments. Its sediment output falls into five size classes: primary clay, silt and sand, and small and large aggregates. That lets it calculate the selective transport and enrichment of fine particles.

soil-water-026.title: The tipping point where a rill is born
soil-water-026.text: A rill starts at a tipping point. Rill initiation is the moment when the shear stress of runoff exceeds the soil's {{ref:soil-phys-101}} and water begins to tear particles loose. Sandy and loamy soils are especially prone to rills, while dense clays resist them. Slope steepness mainly controls whether rills form and how deep they cut. Slope length and soil permeability set how many form. Each soil has a threshold slope below which rills cannot form. On many non-cohesive slopes it is about 2 degrees, at a shear velocity of 3 to 3.5 cm/s. Once rills exist, their walls add to the loss. Up to 37% of erosion in rilled areas may come from collapsing sidewalls undercut and weakened by water.

soil-water-005.title: Sheet erosion, the thin film that strips a field
soil-water-005.text: One rainstorm can remove up to a hundred tons of fine particles per acre from a freshly plowed field, without cutting a single channel. Sheet erosion is the even erosion of soil or other material across a wide area by a thin, unchanneled layer of flowing water. It works in two steps. Rainsplash loosens small particles, as in {{ref:soil-water-004}}, and then a thin, uniform sheet flow carries them a short distance. Each event moves material only a short way, but frequent repetition makes up for the small change per episode. It is common on freshly plowed fields and on bare, unconsolidated ground. On an uneven hillslope it may give way to erosion in rills, which can merge into gullies.

soil-water-042.title: The P factor, credit for conservation practices
soil-water-042.text: Stone walls and hedgerows held soil in place long before anyone wrote an equation for erosion. The support practice factor is the P factor of the Universal Soil Loss Equation, a soil loss ratio expressing how much conservation practices reduce erosion. It is hard to determine because regional maps of conservation practices are usually lacking, so it is often estimated from land use and slope. Field boundaries such as stone walls, hedgerows, earth banks and {{ref:soil-agri-081}} effectively prevented or reduced erosion in pre-industrial farming. A European P-factor model was built from a survey that recorded stone walls and grass margins, and landscape archaeology mapping can fill gaps in the data.

soil-water-256.title: Rainfall simulators, storms on demand
soil-water-256.text: Natural rain cannot be summoned for an experiment, so researchers make their own. A rainfall simulator is a device used in soil science and hydrology to study how soil reacts to rainfall. Simulated rain speeds the study of erosion, surface runoff and leaching. The first, in the 1930s, were sprinkling cans or pipes with holes. In the 1960s, nozzles matched raindrop size, impact speed and evenness, and in the 1980s valves let the intensity vary. In the early 1990s, simulators were used in the US Water Erosion Prediction Project to update the Universal Soil Loss Equation. On bare soil, drop size and terminal velocity must be simulated accurately, because they control splash erosion.

soil-water-258.title: Steadying burned slopes before the rains come
soil-water-258.text: In 2018, after the Thomas Fire in California, floods and flows of mud and debris killed 20 people and destroyed 300 houses. Fire burns canopy, litter, fine roots and soil organic compounds, leaving the soil less protected, less stable and more water-repellent, like the {{ref:soil-phys-034}} described earlier. Post-fire hillslope stabilization covers treatments that offset this damage, to cut the risk of damaging runoff and erosion downhill. Seeding and mulching cover the soil. Surfactants and flocculants counter water repellency and lost aggregation. Contour barriers of logs or straw shorten the slope length. Risk peaks in the first year, so the work must be quick. In the USA, seeding fell from 75% of treated burned areas in the 1970s and 1980s to 30% in the 2000s.

soil-water-039.title: Measuring how far the plow drags a field
soil-water-039.text: A few buried tracers can reveal how far cultivation drags a field downhill. Tillage erosion measurement covers two approaches: tracking the soil that cultivation moves, or measuring where soil is lost and gained. To track movement, researchers mix point or bulk tracers into plots and compare their positions before and after the pass. Losses and gains show up as changes in surface elevation. These are compared against an uneroded fence line or hedgerow, or surveyed with RTK GPS or photogrammetry. Changes in soil organic matter can also signal loss, but so many other factors affect it that the method is unreliable. Since the 1980s, radioisotopes such as Cs-137 and Pb-210 have given much more accurate erosion estimates.

soil-water-040.title: Computer models of soil on the move
soil-water-040.text: Tillage erosion models are computer models that simulate how cultivation moves soil along a hillslope or across a field. The simplest are one-dimensional hillslope models such as TEP and TillERI. They use slope length, gradient and the erosivity of the operation to give erosion rates and risk. WaTEM calculates both water and tillage erosion on a digital elevation model. It treats the soil shifted by each pass as diffusion in the steepest-slope direction. Field-scale models such as SORET and TillEM add the direction of cultivation, moving soil both parallel and perpendicular to it.

soil-water-044.title: The erosion index and highly erodible land
soil-water-044.text: The erosion index, also called the erodibility index, compares how fast a soil could erode with how fast it can afford to. It is potential erosion from all sources except gullies, divided by the soil's T value, the erosion rate above which long-term productivity may suffer. It is used for U.S. conservation compliance and for the Conservation Reserve Program, which requires land to have an index above 8. In the United States, farmers cultivating highly erodible land often must follow a conservation plan to qualify for agricultural assistance.

soil-water-046.title: Sediment, loose grains on their way somewhere
soil-water-046.text: A beach, a dune and a glacier's moraine are all made of the same kind of thing. Sediment is solid material made of loose particles that is carried to a new place and deposited there. It is produced by {{ref:soil-found-052}} and erosion and moved by wind, water, ice or gravity. Water moves it most often, through what geologists call fluvial processes. Beach sands and river deposits are fluvial; dunes and loess are windblown; moraines and till are carried by ice. Once buried, sand and silt can be lithified, hardened into sedimentary rocks such as sandstone and siltstone. Sediment is classified by grain size, shape and composition. Size is measured on the phi scale, a log base 2 scale running from colloid to boulder. The word clay is ambiguous here, because it names both a size range and a group of minerals. Seas and lakes accumulate terrigenous sediment, washed from land mostly by rivers, along with sediment formed in the water, often by organisms. Lake bed sediments that have not yet hardened into rock hold a record of past climates.

soil-water-002.title: Erosion, the great mover of the Earth's surface
soil-water-002.text: Eroded material may travel only a few millimeters, or for thousands of kilometers. Erosion is the removal of soil, rock or dissolved material from one place on the Earth's surface, by processes such as flowing water or wind. The material is carried to another place and deposited there. Movement is what sets it apart from weathering, which moves nothing. Removing material as clastic sediment, made of broken fragments, is physical or mechanical erosion. Removing it by dissolution is {{ref:soil-water-008}}. The agents are many: rainfall, river flow, waves, glaciers, flooding, wind, groundwater, and mass movements such as {{ref:soil-water-057}} and {{ref:soil-water-252}}. Physical erosion is usually fastest on steep slopes. Its rate also responds to rainfall, storminess, wind speed, wave fetch and temperature. The journey ends in deposition, when the material arrives and settles at a new location. For soil, the balance matters. Where erosion outpaces soil formation, it destroys the soil. Slower erosion can still prevent soil features that need time to develop. Inceptisols form on eroded landscapes that, if stable, would have developed into Alfisols.
